definition: Carp means to complain or find fault repeatedly, especially about small things.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word carp. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know carp should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: At every homeowners' meeting, Mr. Bell found something fresh to carp about — the newsletter's font, the sprinklers' angle, the shade of the mulch.
A grumble is milder than carping — one muttered protest and it is over.
A rant is louder and harsher than carping: carping stays a drizzle of small complaints, while a rant delivers the whole storm at once.

To grouse is to grumble aloud about a standing gripe — the schedule, the weather, the boss — usually the same complaint each time it surfaces. To carp is busier and pettier: it keeps finding fresh trifles, one after another, and will not let the list end.

To nitpick is to hunt for tiny flaws — a comma, a smudge, a crooked label — usually while inspecting someone else's work. To carp is to voice complaints aloud and keep voicing them; a nitpicker examines, while a carper keeps up the grievance.
to praise something with unguarded enthusiasm
to accept without objection
Old Norse karpa, 'to brag or wrangle,' left carp as its only common English descendant. The identical-looking fish name arrived separately from Latin carpa, so even the pond offers no true relative.
Carp means to complain or find fault repeatedly, especially about small things.
At every homeowners' meeting, Mr.
Bell found something fresh to carp about — the newsletter's font, the sprinklers' angle, the shade of the mulch.
For six hundred miles Uncle Ray carped from the passenger seat: the radio was a notch too loud, the exits arrived too fast, the map was folded against its creases.
No single objection amounted to anything; the trip still aged everyone a year.
To carp is not to lodge one complaint — it is to keep complaining, always about trifles.
That pettiness separates it from protest, which aims at something large, and from criticize, which can be fair and even useful.
Carp is the word for steady, small-bore complaining — it usually travels with 'about' and a list of trifles.
One muttered objection is a grumble; a sustained blast is a rant.
Its unit neighbor vex names what all that carping eventually does to the listener.

Every rehearsal of the spring play came with a soundtrack: the assistant director's running commentary of complaints.
Monday it was the angle of a hat brim.
Tuesday, the length of a pause.
Wednesday, the color of the tickets — which the audience would be holding in the dark.
The lead actress finally named the pattern: he did not object to anything in particular; he simply needed to carp, and any trifle would do.
Meanwhile the real problem — a second act that ran forty minutes long — went unmentioned all season.
On opening night the reviews praised the hats, the pauses, and the tickets, and complained about only one thing: the length.
